claim: Object Ownership has three settings: Bucket owner enforced (ACLs disabled, bucket owner owns every object), Bucket owner preferred (bucket owner owns new objects written with the bucket-owner-full-control canned ACL), and Object writer (the uploading account owns the object and can grant access with ACLs).
question: What are the three Object Ownership settings, and who owns uploaded objects under each?

values.display: Bucket owner enforced (default)
Bucket owner preferred
Object writer
bucket-owner-full-control

evidence.quote: **Bucket owner enforced (default)** – ACLs are disabled, and the bucket owner automatically owns and has full control over every object in the bucket. ACLs no longer affect permissions to data in the S3 bucket. The bucket uses policies to define access control.
**Bucket owner preferred** – The bucket owner owns and has full control over new objects that other accounts write to the bucket with the `bucket-owner-full-control` canned ACL.
**Object writer** – The AWS account that uploads an object owns the object, has full control over it, and can grant other users access to it through ACLs.

claim: ACLs can be disabled on new and existing buckets. On an existing bucket with objects, after ACLs are disabled the bucket and object ACLs no longer take part in access evaluation and access is decided by policies; ACLs can be re-enabled later and the earlier ACLs come back.
question: What happens to existing object ACLs when you disable ACLs on a bucket?

values.display: the object and bucket ACLs are no longer part of an access evaluation
your preexisting bucket and object ACLs are restored

evidence.quote: You can disable ACLs on both newly created and already existing buckets. For newly created buckets, ACLs are disabled by default. In the case of an existing bucket that already has objects in it, after you disable ACLs, the object and bucket ACLs are no longer part of an access evaluation, and access is granted or denied on the basis of policies. For existing buckets, you can re-enable ACLs at any time after you disable them, and your preexisting bucket and object ACLs are restored.

claim: With ACLs disabled, a bucket accepts only PUT requests that specify no ACL or the bucket-owner-full-control ACL; a PUT with any other ACL fails with a 400 error and the code AccessControlListNotSupported.
question: Which uploads does a bucket with ACLs disabled reject?

values.display: accepts only PUT requests that do not specify an ACL or PUT requests with bucket owner full control ACLs
fail and return a 400 error with the error code AccessControlListNotSupported

qualifiers.condition: Object Ownership set to Bucket owner enforced

evidence.quote: After you disable ACLs, your bucket accepts only `PUT` requests that do not specify an ACL or `PUT` requests with bucket owner full control ACLs, for example, the `bucket-owner-full-control` canned ACL or equivalent forms of this ACL expressed in XML. Existing applications that support bucket owner full control ACLs see no impact. `PUT` requests that contain other ACLs (for example, custom grants to certain AWS accounts) fail and return a `400` error with the error code `AccessControlListNotSupported`.

claim: By default S3 replicates metadata such as tags, ACLs and Object Lock settings from the source object to its replicas only. With replica modification sync enabled on both buckets, metadata changes made on a replica are copied back to the source, making replication two-way.
question: Are changes made to a replica's tags or ACLs copied back to the source object?

values.display: replicates metadata from the source objects to the replicas only
replica modification sync
making the replication bidirectional (two-way replication)

qualifiers.condition: replica modification sync must be enabled on both source and destination buckets

evidence.quote: By default, Amazon S3 replicates metadata from the source objects to the replicas only. When replica modification sync is enabled, Amazon S3 replicates metadata changes made to the replica copies back to the source object, making the replication bidirectional (two-way replication).

You must enable replica modification sync on both the source and destination buckets to replicate replica metadata changes like object access control lists (ACLs), object tags, object annotations, or Object Lock settings on the replicated objects.

claim: Uploading an object with a key that already exists in a versioning-enabled bucket creates another version instead of replacing the existing object. A bucket can hold an unlimited number of objects, and you need write permission on the bucket to upload.
question: What happens when you upload to an existing key in a versioned bucket?

values.display: creates another version of the object instead of replacing the existing object
an unlimited number of objects in a bucket

evidence.quote: If you upload an object with a key name that already exists in a versioning-enabled bucket, Amazon S3 creates another version of the object instead of replacing the existing object.

Objects consist of the file data and metadata that describes the object. You can have an unlimited number of objects in a bucket. Before you can upload files to an Amazon S3 bucket, you need write permissions for the bucket.

claim: Starting a multipart upload returns an upload ID that every later part upload, list, complete or stop request must carry; anonymous users cannot initiate multipart uploads.
question: Can an anonymous user start a multipart upload?

values.display: anonymous users cannot initiate multipart uploads
this upload ID is required when you upload parts, list parts, complete an upload, or stop an upload

evidence.quote: Amazon S3 will then return a response with an upload ID, which is a unique identifier for your multipart upload. This upload ID is required when you upload parts, list parts, complete an upload, or stop an upload. If you want to provide metadata describing the object being uploaded, you must provide it in the request to initiate the multipart upload. Anonymous users cannot initiate multipart uploads.

claim: A directory bucket in an Availability Zone with no request activity for at least 90 days becomes inactive and is temporarily unreadable and unwritable; it keeps all data and metadata, storage charges continue, and an access request reactivates it, typically within a few minutes, with HTTP 503 errors during the transition.
question: What happens to a directory bucket that is not used for a long time?

values.display: transition to an inactive state
inactive buckets retain all storage, object metadata, and bucket metadata
reads and writes return an HTTP 503 (Service Unavailable) error code

qualifiers.condition: no request activity for at least 90 days; does not apply to Local Zone buckets

evidence.quote: Directory buckets in Availability Zones that have no request activity for a period of at least 90 days transition to an inactive state. While in an inactive state, a directory bucket is temporarily inaccessible for reads and writes. Inactive buckets retain all storage, object metadata, and bucket metadata. Existing storage charges apply to inactive buckets. If you make an access request to an inactive bucket, the bucket transitions to an active state, typically within a few minutes. During this transition period, reads and writes return an HTTP `503 (Service Unavailable)` error code. This doesn't apply to buckets in Local Zones.

claim: Directory buckets have all Block Public Access settings on, Object Ownership set to bucket owner enforced and ACLs disabled, and these settings cannot be modified. Users have no permissions on directory buckets by default; access is granted with IAM identities or access points.
question: Which access settings on a directory bucket are fixed?

values.display: these settings can't be modified
by default, users don't have permissions for directory buckets

evidence.quote: Directory buckets have all S3 Block Public Access settings enabled by default at the bucket level. S3 Object Ownership is set to bucket owner enforced and access control lists (ACLs) are disabled. These settings can't be modified.

By default, users don't have permissions for directory buckets. To grant access permissions for directory buckets, you can use IAM to create users, groups, or roles and attach permissions to those identities.

claim: For data residency, a directory bucket can be created in a single AWS Dedicated Local Zone to keep data inside a specific data perimeter; directory buckets in Local Zones support the S3 One Zone-IA storage class, and Local Zones are supported only for directory buckets.
question: Which bucket type supports data residency in a Dedicated Local Zone?

values.display: a directory bucket in a single AWS Dedicated Local Zone (DLZ)
Local Zones are only supported for directory buckets not general purpose buckets

evidence.quote: For data-residency use cases, you can create a directory bucket in a single AWS Dedicated Local Zone (DLZ) to store data. In Dedicated Local Zones, you can create S3 directory buckets to store data in a specific data perimeter, which helps support your data residency and isolation use cases. Directory buckets in Local Zones support the S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA; Z-IA) storage class.
**AWS Local Zones** – Local Zones are only supported for directory buckets not general purpose buckets.

claim: S3 has four bucket types: general purpose, directory, table and vector buckets. Table buckets store tabular data as Apache Iceberg tables for analytics engines such as Athena, Redshift and Spark; vector buckets store and query vector embeddings with dedicated APIs.
question: What are S3 table buckets and vector buckets for?

values.display: four types of buckets—general purpose buckets, directory buckets, table buckets, and vector buckets
purpose-built for storing tabular data in the Apache Iceberg format
purpose-built to store and query vectors

evidence.quote: Amazon S3 supports four types of buckets—general purpose buckets, directory buckets, table buckets, and vector buckets. Each type of bucket provides a unique set of features for different use cases.

S3 Tables are purpose-built for storing tabular data in the Apache Iceberg format. You can query tabular data in S3 Tables with popular query engines, including Amazon Athena, Amazon Redshift, and Apache Spark.

**Vector buckets** – S3 vector buckets are a type of Amazon S3 bucket that are purpose-built to store and query vectors. Vector buckets use dedicated API operations to write and query vector data efficiently.

note: Table and vector buckets are newer than the SAA-C03 guide; the changes lens decides whether they are examinable.
